newsitem.title: UK: Britain's House of Lords may face standards review.
newsitem.headline: Britain's House of Lords may face standards review.

text.p: Britain's House of Lords (upper house of parliament) could find its standards of conduct under investigation by the committee which has already examined the House of Commons, the Times reported on Tuesday.

A spokesman for the Nolan Committee said on Monday he would not rule out "looking at arrangements in the House of Lords", but added that it was "certainly not something we're going to do in the short term".
The Times said the committee, chaired by Lord Nolan, was likely to review the Lords when it reconvened in October.
The Nolan Committee spokesman said that "possibly then or sometime later on" the Lords might be covered by the committee.
But he added that it was "a question of not ruling something out rather than ruling something in."
Currently, registering interests in the upper House is largely voluntary, while in the Commons tough regulations have been introduced to ensure transparency.
The Times said barely half of the 600 members of the upper house who attended regularly had listed any consultancies or directorships in the latest register.
The Nolan Committee was set up by former prime minister John Major following a spate of allegations of financial misconduct by members of parliament.

The opposition Conservatives have hounded the new Labour government recently over shareholdings in British Petroleum ) held by the company's former chairman Lord David Simon, who is now a minister in the government.

Lord Simon decided to sell the two million pounds ($3.2 million) shareholding earlier this month after a political row in which the Conservatives claimed his impartiality as a minister would be at risk.
The Independent newspaper said in its Tuesday edition that he was to give the proceeds of the share sale to fund places at an independent school.
That could prove a further embarrassment for the government, the newspaper said, as it was just moving to abolish state subsidies for private education.
The Nolan Committee consists of a team of lawyers, academics, industrialists, diplomats and politicians.
Lord Nolan is expected to stand down from the committee at the end of October.
